It contrasts God's responsive call with the complete nonresponse of those invoked besides Him.

It declares that those called besides God have no power to remove or redirect harm.
It challenges the worshippers' failure to bring authority for gods besides God, adding an evidentiary critique.
Those called as alleged partners do not answer, making visible the futility of their invocation.
It identifies God as the true reality and what is invoked besides Him as false, stating the theological contrast behind the rebuke.

It condemns calling on another god without proof, supplying an epistemic boundary for the worship challenged here.
It rejects gods that create nothing and cannot control harm, benefit, death, life, or resurrection.
The idolaters' answer that they worship their gods introduces the same inquiry found in Abraham's confrontation.

His declaration of enmity toward all objects except the Lord of the worlds gives the positive boundary of the rebuke.

The question whether another god can create alongside God invites the rational comparison absent from idol worship.

It asks whether any alleged partners can perform any part of God's acts of creation, provision, death, or life.

It says they do not hear invocation and could not answer it, an especially close parallel to the focus's challenge.
